sample_tweets.text: 🏥🔓 **CARECLOUD DATA BREACH IMPACTS 3.75 MILLION PEOPLE — ATTACKERS ACCESSED HEALTHCARE COMPANY'S AWS ENVIRONMENT**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🏥 Healthcare Security · August 19, 2026**  🎯 **A healthcare technology breach disclosed earlier this year is much larger than initially understood.**  U.S. healthtech company:  🏥 **CareCloud**  has confirmed that approximately:  🔥 **3,756,469 individuals**  were affected by a cybersecurity incident.  ### 🏥 WHY CARECLOUD MATTERS  CareCloud provides technology used for:  📋 electronic health records 💳 medical billing 🏥 practice management 💰 healthcare revenue-cycle services.  That places the company directly inside the technology infrastructure supporting medical organizations and patient information.  ### ☁️ ATTACKERS ACCESSED AN AWS ENVIRONMENT  The incident occurred between:  📅 March 10 and 📅 March 16, 2026.  According to breach notifications:  ☠️ an unauthorized third party accessed one of CareCloud's AWS environments  and claimed to have:  📤 **exfiltrated database information.**  ### 💥 THE ATTACK ALSO CAUSED DISRUPTION  CareCloud originally disclosed the incident in March.  The cyberattack caused approximately:  ⏱️ **8 hours of network disruption**  and temporarily cut access to one database.  ### 👥 3,756,469 PEOPLE  CareCloud's report to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services now places the affected population at:  🔥 **3.756 million individuals.**  That's a major healthcare privacy incident.  ### 🔐 WHAT DATA WAS EXPOSED?  CareCloud's publicly available sample notification confirms:  👤 full names  but does not publicly specify every additional data category involved for all affected people.  So it would be inaccurate to invent specific medical or financial fields without evidence.  ### 🎣 THE NEXT THREAT — PHISHING  Large healthcare breaches can feed highly convincing:  🎣 phishing attacks 📧 impersonation ☎️ fraud 🪪 identity-based social engineering.  Victims may not even recognize the CareCloud name because CareCloud often provides backend technology to healthcare organizations rather than directly interacting with individual patients.  ### 🛡️ RESPONSE  CareCloud began sending breach notifications in July.  Affected recipients are being offered identity-protection services.  At the time of BleepingComputer's reporting:  ⚠️ no ransomware or extortion group had publicly claimed responsibility.  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🔴 3,756,469 people affected 🔴 AWS environment accessed 🔴 Databases reportedly exfiltrated 🔴 Eight-hour network disruption 🏥 Healthcare ecosystem impacted 📨 Victim notifications distributed ⚠️ No ransomware gang publicly claimed attack  The important lesson:  > **Healthcare organizations increasingly depend on technology providers that can become one breach away from exposing information belonging to millions of patients they never directly interacted with.**  🔗 **Sources:** BleepingComputer • CareCloud • U.S. HHS  #CyberSecurity #CareCloud #Healthcare #DataBreach #AWS #CloudSecurity #PatientData #ThreatIntelligence #CyberNews

🇯🇵🔓 **JAPANESE CLOUD GIANT SAKURA INTERNET HACKED — UP TO 1.36 MILLION ACCOUNTS POTENTIALLY EXPOSED**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · ☁️ Cloud Security · August 19, 2026**  🎯 **A cyberattack against one of Japan's strategically important cloud and data-center providers may have affected more than one million customer accounts.**  Japanese infrastructure provider:  🌸 **Sakura Internet**  has disclosed unauthorized access to an internal sales-management system containing customer contract and membership information.  Potential impact:  🔥 **up to 1,360,563 accounts**  ### ☁️ THIS ISN'T A SMALL HOSTING COMPANY  Sakura Internet provides:  🌐 web hosting 🖥️ VPS services ☁️ public cloud 🏢 data-center infrastructure 🤖 GPU computing.  It has also been selected as a domestic provider supporting:  🇯🇵 **Japan's Government Cloud program**  making the company strategically important to Japan's push for domestic cloud infrastructure.  ### 🔎 HOW THE BIGGER INCIDENT WAS DISCOVERED  Attackers accessed Sakura's IT environment on:  📅 **August 9**  But investigators uncovered the larger exposure while investigating a separate compromise involving the company's:  🌐 Sakura Rental Server service.  That earlier incident involved:  🔴 unauthorized access to 583 accounts 🔴 customer-facing systems 🔴 access to client information 🔴 malware installed inside Sakura's environment.  Investigators then discovered the much larger potential exposure.  ### 📊 UP TO 1.36 MILLION ACCOUNTS  Sakura says:  🔥 **1,360,563 accounts**  may have been affected.  However:  ⚠️ the investigation remains ongoing ⚠️ the exact number isn't final ⚠️ data exfiltration has not been confirmed.  ### 🔐 WHAT ABOUT PASSWORDS AND CREDIT CARDS?  The company says:  🔐 stored passwords are hashed  and:  💳 the compromised system does **not** store credit-card information.  That limits some potential impact but does not remove the privacy risk associated with customer and contract information.  ### 🦠 MALWARE WAS FOUND  Sakura confirmed malware had been installed during the broader incident.  The company:  ✅ invalidated abused credentials ✅ removed the malware ✅ informed relevant authorities ✅ began notifying affected customers.  An August 20 update added another important clarification:  ⚠️ **Sakura says the incident was not ransomware and no ransom demand was made.**  The company has not publicly identified the malware involved.  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🔴 Sakura Internet compromised 🔴 Internal IT system accessed 🔴 Malware discovered 🔴 Up to 1.36 million accounts potentially affected 🔴 Earlier compromise involved 583 accounts 🟢 Abused credentials invalidated 🟢 Malware removed 🟢 Credit-card data not stored in affected system ⚠️ Data exfiltration not yet confirmed ⚠️ Incident explicitly confirmed as non-ransomware  The bigger concern:  > **Cloud providers don't only host customer infrastructure — they also become highly valuable concentration points for customer identities, contracts and administrative data.**  🔗 **Sources:** BleepingComputer • Sakura Internet  #CyberSecurity #DataBreach #SakuraInternet #Japan #CloudSecurity #Malware #ThreatIntelligence #CyberNews

🤖🚨 **CHATGPT HIT BY MAJOR GLOBAL OUTAGE — LOGINS, SIGNUPS, CHATS, CODEX AND OPENAI API SERVICES DISRUPTED**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · ☁️ Cloud / AI Availability · August 19, 2026**  🎯 **A major OpenAI outage disrupted ChatGPT and several connected services worldwide.**  The incident began at approximately:  🕗 **8:00 PM ET**  Users in regions including:  🇺🇸 United States 🇪🇺 Europe  reported being unable to:  ❌ sign into ChatGPT ❌ create new accounts ❌ load previous conversations ❌ send messages ❌ properly load the ChatGPT interface.  Some users encountered:  ⚠️ **“too many concurrent requests”**  errors.  ### 🤖 CHATGPT WASN'T THE ONLY SERVICE AFFECTED  The disruption also affected:  💻 **OpenAI Codex**  and:  🌐 **OpenAI API services**  BleepingComputer reported that as many as:  🔥 **12 API endpoints**  were showing issues on OpenAI's status infrastructure.  ### 🔎 OPENAI ACKNOWLEDGED THE INCIDENT  OpenAI confirmed that users were experiencing login problems across impacted services.  The company identified the incident shortly after it began and started deploying mitigation measures.  ### 🏢 WHY AN AI OUTAGE MATTERS TO ENTERPRISES  AI platforms are becoming integrated into:  👨‍💻 software development 📊 analytics 🤖 automation 📝 documentation 🎧 customer support 🔎 research ⚙️ operational workflows.  That means a widespread AI-platform outage increasingly resembles a traditional SaaS outage.  Organizations dependent on one AI provider can suddenly lose access to workflows that employees increasingly expect to be continuously available.  ### 🧠 CYBERSECURITY CLARIFICATION  At the time of the reporting:  ⚠️ **There was no evidence presented that the outage was caused by a cyberattack.**  Availability incidents can result from many causes.  So:  ❌ outage ≠ breach ❌ service failure ≠ DDoS unless evidence supports it  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🔴 Major ChatGPT outage 🔴 Logins affected 🔴 New signups affected 🔴 Existing chats failed to load 🔴 Codex affected 🔴 Multiple OpenAI API endpoints affected 🌍 Users worldwide reported problems 🛠️ OpenAI acknowledged the incident ⚠️ No cyberattack cause established in the reporting  The bigger resilience lesson:  > **As AI becomes infrastructure, organizations need to think about AI-provider availability the same way they think about cloud, identity and communications outages.**  🔗 **Source:** BleepingComputer • OpenAI Status  #CyberSecurity #ChatGPT #OpenAI #AI #Outage #CloudSecurity #Resilience #CyberNews

🎮💥 **MICROSOFT INVESTIGATES AUGUST WINDOWS UPDATE AFTER GAMES BEGIN CRASHING, FREEZING AND REBOOTING PCs**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🪟 Windows · August 20, 2026**  🎯 **Microsoft's August 2026 Windows updates are creating another problem — this time for gamers.**  Microsoft says it is investigating reports that updates released beginning with:  ⚙️ **KB5121003**  may prevent certain games from launching correctly or cause them to crash on:  🪟 Windows 11 24H2 🪟 Windows 11 25H2  Affected users have reported:  🔴 games freezing 🔴 games closing unexpectedly 🔴 EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION errors 🔴 unexpected Windows restarts  ### 🎮 WHICH GAMES HAVE BEEN REPORTED?  BleepingComputer says reported titles include:  🎮 ARC Raiders 🥊 MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls 🔥 The Finals  Microsoft says only a limited number of games appear affected so far.  ### 🔄 THE PROBLEM FOLLOWED PATCH TUESDAY  The issue began appearing after Microsoft released:  📅 August 11, 2026 🔧 KB5121003 and later updates  as part of the August Patch Tuesday cycle.  That month's security release itself was substantial.  Microsoft patched approximately:  🚨 **400 vulnerabilities**  including:  🔥 one actively exploited vulnerability ⚠️ two publicly disclosed zero-days.  So organizations face the familiar security-versus-stability problem:  > **Security updates need to be deployed quickly — but regressions can still affect production systems.**  ### 🔎 MICROSOFT IS INVESTIGATING  Microsoft says it is still determining whether the Windows updates are directly responsible.  Users experiencing the issue have been asked to submit diagnostic information through Microsoft's Feedback Hub.  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🟠 August Windows updates under investigation 🎮 Several games affected 💥 Crashes and freezes reported 🔄 Unexpected PC restarts possible 🪟 Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2 involved ⚠️ Root cause not yet formally confirmed 🔧 Microsoft investigating  This isn't a cyberattack.  But it demonstrates another reality of security operations:  > **Patch management isn't simply “install everything immediately.” Enterprises also need testing, rollback planning and visibility into regressions caused by security updates.**  🔗 **Source:** BleepingComputer • Microsoft  #CyberSecurity #Microsoft #Windows11 #PatchTuesday #WindowsUpdate #SysAdmin #CyberNews

🛡️💥 **MICROSOFT DEFENDER UPDATE CAUSES QUICK, FULL AND OFFLINE VIRUS SCANS TO FAIL ON SOME WINDOWS SYSTEMS**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🪟 Endpoint Security · August 20, 2026**  🎯 **Imagine launching your antivirus scan—and the antivirus engine itself stops working.**  That's what some Microsoft Defender users have been reporting following recent:  🔄 **Security Intelligence updates.**  Affected users reported problems involving:  🔴 Quick Scan 🔴 Full Scan 🔴 Defender Offline Scan  with scans failing or Defender's antimalware process stopping unexpectedly.  ### 💥 WHAT USERS REPORTED  Affected systems may begin scanning normally before Defender encounters an error.  Some systems then display messages indicating that:  ⚠️ the threat service stopped  and request that the service be restarted.  ### 🧠 IMPORTANT — THIS DOESN'T AUTOMATICALLY MEAN MALWARE  Security software unexpectedly shutting down naturally looks suspicious.  But:  ❌ Defender crashing ≠ evidence malware disabled Defender.  The issue has been reported across otherwise clean systems following updates.  That strongly points toward a software/update regression for affected installations.  ### 🔄 TIMELINE  Reports began appearing after security-intelligence updates distributed around:  📅 **August 18**  Multiple users subsequently reported similar scanning failures.  ### 🟢 NEWER DEFINITIONS APPEAR TO FIX IT  More recent Defender intelligence updates reportedly restore normal scanning on many affected machines.  For defenders, the sensible response is:  ✅ install the newest Microsoft Defender intelligence update ✅ verify real-time protection status ✅ verify a Quick Scan completes ✅ investigate separately if genuine compromise indicators exist  ### 🏢 WHY SOC TEAMS CARE  Microsoft Defender operates across enormous numbers of:  💻 Windows endpoints 🏢 corporate laptops 🖥️ enterprise workstations 🔐 managed environments  Even a temporary scanning regression can create:  📈 SOC noise 📞 help-desk tickets ⚠️ endpoint-health uncertainty 🧐 false compromise concerns  ### ⚠️ DON'T MIX DIFFERENT STORIES WITHOUT EVIDENCE  Separate Microsoft Defender vulnerability research has circulated recently.  That does **not automatically prove** those issues caused this scanning problem.  Unless Microsoft or solid technical evidence establishes the connection:  > **correlation should not be presented as causation.**  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🟠 Quick scans affected on some systems 🟠 Full scans affected 🟠 Offline scans affected 🟠 Defender process crashes reported 🟢 Newer intelligence releases reportedly resolve the issue for many users ⚠️ Scanner failure alone does not indicate compromise  This isn't today's biggest cyberattack.  But when one of the world's most widely deployed endpoint-security products starts failing its own malware scans:  > **security teams notice immediately.**  🔗 **Sources:** Cyberpress • Windows Central • community reports  #CyberSecurity #Microsoft #MicrosoftDefender #Windows #EndpointSecurity #EDR #SOC #BlueTeam #CyberNews

Berlin state ministries got cut off from Germany's central government IT network this week after a security breach. Not a minor hiccup. A disconnection significant enough that someone decided the right move was to sever the link entirely, which is the cyber equivalent of containing a fire by pulling down a wall.  No attribution confirmed yet, and we should be honest that confirmed attribution takes time. But let's talk about context, because context is doing a lot of work here.  Germany has been a documented Russian cyber target for years. APT28, also known as Fancy Bear, has been identified by both the BfV (German domestic intelligence) and the BND (foreign intelligence) as a persistent threat to German government networks, political parties, and critical infrastructure. The German government, along with EU and UK partners, has formally co-attributed a Russian FSB cyberattack on Poland's power grid. Russian disinformation campaigns targeting Germany ahead of federal elections have been confirmed by security services as centrally orchestrated from Russia. This is not a theoretical threat landscape. It is a documented, named, ongoing one.  So when Berlin state ministries get isolated from central government IT infrastructure, the question of who did it is not idle speculation. It sits inside an established pattern.  The targeting choice is worth thinking through carefully. State-level ministries in a federal system are an interesting pick. They're not the highest-profile targets, but they're also frequently not as well-resourced defensively as federal infrastructure. They hold sensitive administrative data, internal communications, coordination records. And critically, they're connected to the larger government network, which makes them a potential pathway into that network if the attacker's goal is lateral movement rather than just disruption. The fact that isolation protocols were triggered suggests whoever is managing incident response took that possibility seriously. You don't cut off a ministry from the central network because things look manageable.  This fits a pattern we've been tracking across European governmental infrastructure. Russian military intelligence has been documented using compromised IP cameras to surveil NATO logistics movements. The FSB hit Polish power infrastructure. These aren't one-offs. They're a persistent, grinding campaign against alliance member state systems at multiple levels, federal, state, critical infrastructure, private sector adjacent to government. The variation in targeting keeps defenders spread thin.  The state-level focus specifically deserves more attention than it usually gets. Federal agencies get the security investment and the political attention. State and regional government networks in EU member states are frequently the weak link, and adversaries with enough patience and resources to map out a federal system's architecture know exactly where the softer entry points are. Germany's federal structure means sixteen states, each with their own administrative networks, each a potential approach vector.  The timing matters too. Germany just came through a federal election cycle that attracted significant documented Russian interference activity. Hybrid operations in the Russian playbook don't tend to end cleanly when an election concludes. Cyberattacks combined with disinformation are designed to compound each other: the attack creates a real disruption, the disruption generates news coverage and political noise, and disinformation campaigns shape how that noise is interpreted. The goal isn't just the breach. It's the surrounding effect.  What we don't have yet: confirmed attribution, clarity on which ministries were affected and what data may have been accessed or exfiltrated, and a full picture of how the breach occurred. Forensics takes time and governments are often reluctant to release details that reveal how they were penetrated. So this post will have gaps that only time and official disclosure can fill.  What we do have: a significant enough incident that emergency isolation protocols were activated, occurring in a European capital, against government infrastructure, during a period of well-documented heightened Russian hybrid operations against NATO member states. The operational profile is consistent with previously confirmed Russian APT activity. That doesn't make it confirmed. It makes it the leading hypothesis worth treating seriously while investigation proceeds.  The broader catalog is getting long. Hacked cameras watching NATO supply lines. Power grid attacks. Political party network intrusions. Election interference campaigns. And now Berlin ministries cut off from central government IT. European state-level government networks are being tested repeatedly, and the results of those tests keep suggesting the same thing: the resourcing and defensive posture at sub-national government level across the EU is not keeping pace with what's being thrown at it.  That gap is the actual strategic problem. Individual incidents get covered. The systemic vulnerability underneath them gets a paragraph, maybe two, and then we move on.  foreigninterference.org/post… #foreigninterference #AdvancedPersistentThreatOperations #CyberEspionage #InfrastructureAttacks #PersistentNetworkInfiltration

sample_tweets.text: I'm currently of the mind that it doesn't have to be anonymous as it isn't meant to contend with something like TOR. However 2 hosts operating in the walled garden shouldn't being able to correlate that a user on both of their platforms is the same person. There are some strategies I've heard brainstormed to mitigate non-anonymity but it isn't the problem I want to solve right now. (Not that it isn't important mind you.)  And I'm 100% sure that hosts on the network should not be able to boot people out of the walled garden. I don't intend to give more power to large sites, more take the burden of moderation off small ones. Of course if a user is violating rules of the walled garden (sharing an identity with other people, running unannounced scrapers) that would be grounds for losing access.  I wouldn't want to impose how moderation of a particular host must be done, if they want to ban for particular opinions that's their own (bad) choice. It can't be opinionated on things outside its 'jurisdiction' lest hosts and users won't have incentive to use it.  Hosts should also be allowed to accept connections from outside the walled garden, provided they don't forward those connections into it arbitrarily, or perform arbitrary lookups on their behalf. That would defeat a lot of the utility. This is probably essential to obtain a userbase, it would fracture the web. Right now non-normies are forced to use platforms that normies are on. If the walled garden required hosts reject all connections from outside of it, it would just be immediately killed and non-normies would never have the opportunity to join.  Hosts could still choose whether they support external connections or not, arbitrarily turning it on and off depending on what's happening. Sudden DDOS attack? Just turn off the unprivileged portal. Obviously Cloudflare already does a lot of this so there isn't a huge inventive. But it should be trivial from a technical perspective.  Hosts that don't care to cater to normies and would rather sacrifice quantity for quality would likely opt to operate totally within the walled garden.  Part of my goal is to bring communities that have slipped off the open web into their own smaller walled gardens, back into the open. Forums for example are a big example.   Touching on non-anonymity again, part of my thoughts on it are that outside of using a VPN we are already effectively not anonymous. Governments can subpoena it in the snap of a finger. I'm hoping this design would still allow one to connect to the walled garden using a VPN, but they would still need a 'personalized' id which would need to be turned over. If they did everything right, all that would reveal about them is their VPN connection and the vouch chain for the identity.  Speaking of that, I'm pretty strongly of the opinion the right mechanism for this is vouches. The reason is that if an individual vouches for too many bad actors, they can lose vouch privileges, and everyone they vouched for retroactively needs new vouches to access the garden. This would ripple down, and up, the chain. The principle here is that you can't just vouch for anyone because it reflects back on you. I intend for people to think about who they vouch for, whether they trust them to follow the rules or not.  I initially played with this idea as a way of preventing cheating in online games. I'm sure some of the design reflects that.  It should be obvious, while it isn't anonymous, it wouldn't require government ID to participate. Online games also made it clear that doesn't work anyway, in Korea elderly people just sell their ID to kids, they make a new account and start cheating again.  It isn't infallible but it increases the cost of making sock puppet accounts greatly. That should ultimately be the goal, increase the cost of turnover.  Long winded post, I'll probably do a real write up on it in the future that isn't all over the place and is a bit more concise. If you want to reach out to discuss it on a synchronous medium I would be interested

sample_tweets.text: ☠️🔐 **MICROSOFT ENTRA ID HIT BY A CVSS 10.0 REMOTE-CODE-EXECUTION FLAW — MICROSOFT CONFIRMS EXPLOITATION IN THE WILD**  **CyberSignal Daily ✓ · 🔐 Identity Security · August 21, 2026**  🎯 **Microsoft has disclosed a maximum-severity vulnerability affecting Entra ID — the cloud identity platform formerly known as Azure Active Directory — and says attackers have already exploited the flaw in the wild.**  The vulnerability is:  🔥 **CVE-2026-69836** 🚨 **CVSS: 10.0 / 10.0** ☁️ **Platform: Microsoft Entra ID** 💥 **Impact: Remote Code Execution** 🔓 **Unauthorized attacker: YES** 🌐 **Network attack: YES** ⚠️ **Exploitation in the wild: CONFIRMED**  There is one very important piece of good news:  🟢 **Microsoft says the vulnerability has already been fully mitigated.**  According to Microsoft:  > **No customer action is currently required.**  But the combination of:  **Identity platform + remote code execution + CVSS 10.0 + confirmed exploitation**  makes this one of the most important security disclosures of August 21.  ### 🔐 FIRST — WHAT IS MICROSOFT ENTRA ID?  Microsoft Entra ID is the identity and access-management service previously called:  **Azure Active Directory / Azure AD**  Organizations use it for:  👤 user identities 🔐 authentication ☁️ cloud application access 🧑‍💼 workforce identities 🛡️ access policies 🔗 single sign-on 🔑 authorization 📱 Microsoft 365 access ☁️ Azure access 🌐 third-party application authentication  Identity infrastructure sits at the center of modern enterprise security.  An endpoint compromise can affect one machine.  An identity-system compromise can potentially affect access to **many systems at once**.  That's why a maximum-severity flaw in a cloud identity platform immediately deserves attention.  ### 💥 THE VULNERABILITY — UNSAFE DESERIALIZATION  Microsoft describes CVE-2026-69836 as involving:  🔥 **deserialization of untrusted data**  Conceptually, serialization takes an object or structured information and converts it into a form that can be stored or transmitted.  Deserialization reverses that process.  The security problem appears when:  Attacker-controlled input ↓ Application accepts it ↓ Application reconstructs an object ↓ Unsafe behavior becomes possible  If untrusted serialized content is processed incorrectly, consequences can include:  ☠️ arbitrary code execution 🚫 denial-of-service 🔓 access-control bypass ⚙️ unauthorized application behavior  Microsoft's security advisory says the vulnerability could allow an **unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network**.  That is why the flaw received the maximum possible:  🚨 **CVSS 10.0**  ### 🌐 THIS WASN'T ONLY THEORETICAL  Microsoft says:  🔥 **CVE-2026-69836 has been exploited in the wild.**  That distinction matters.  Security vulnerabilities generally fall into several operational categories:  1️⃣ theoretically exploitable 2️⃣ proof-of-concept exists 3️⃣ exploitation attempts observed 4️⃣ confirmed real-world exploitation  CVE-2026-69836 is already in the most serious category.  It means defenders are not discussing what an attacker **might** eventually attempt.  Microsoft says exploitation has already occurred.  ### ❓ BUT WE DON'T YET KNOW WHO DID IT  There is still a significant intelligence gap.  As of THN's August 21 report, Microsoft has not publicly detailed:  ❓ who exploited CVE-2026-69836 ❓ what organizations were targeted ❓ when exploitation began ❓ how widespread the activity became ❓ what post-exploitation actions occurred ❓ whether the attackers were financially motivated ❓ whether a nation-state actor was involved  This is important.  **Confirmed exploitation does not automatically mean widespread mass exploitation.**  It could involve:  one campaign a small number of targets targeted espionage limited research activity or broader malicious exploitation.  Until Microsoft releases more information, strong attribution claims would be speculation.  ### 🛡️ MICROSOFT SAYS IT HAS ALREADY FIXED IT  Unlike an ordinary Patch Tuesday vulnerability, Microsoft says customers don't need to install anything for this flaw.  Microsoft's statement:  🟢 vulnerability fully mitigated 🟢 no action required from Entra ID customers  Why?  Because Entra ID is a **Microsoft-operated cloud service**.  Microsoft controls the underlying infrastructure and can deploy server-side mitigations without every organization individually updating software.  This demonstrates one security advantage of managed cloud services:  When the provider can patch centrally:  Microsoft discovers problem ↓ Microsoft deploys mitigation ↓ cloud service changes globally ↓ customers inherit the fix  Instead of:  vendor releases patch ↓ thousands of companies receive notification ↓ change-control meeting ↓ testing ↓ maintenance window ↓ deployment ↓ some systems remain forgotten  ### ⚠️ BUT “NO ACTION REQUIRED” DOES NOT MEAN “IGNORE THE INCIDENT”  For security teams, Microsoft's statement means:  **There is no patch administrators need to deploy.**  It does **not** necessarily mean:  > “The incident has no security significance.”  A SOC may still want to evaluate:  🔎 unusual Entra ID authentication events 🔎 unexpected privileged activity 🔎 anomalous cloud application access 🔎 identity configuration changes 🔎 unusual administrative actions 🔎 suspicious token usage 🔎 access from abnormal locations 🔎 unexpected changes occurring around the exploitation timeframe  Because there is an important difference between:  🛡️ **the vulnerability is fixed**  and:  🔎 **we know no attacker touched our environment.**  Microsoft has not publicly supplied enough exploitation detail in THN's report to define a complete threat-hunting profile for the activity.  ### 🏢 WHY IDENTITY SYSTEMS ARE SO VALUABLE  Modern enterprise architecture increasingly looks like this:  Employee ↓ Identity provider ↓ Microsoft 365 ↓ Azure ↓ SaaS applications ↓ internal applications ↓ cloud infrastructure  The identity provider becomes the gateway.  That makes identity systems attractive targets because attackers can potentially avoid repeatedly attacking individual applications.  Instead they focus on:  🔑 credentials 🎟️ tokens 🪪 identities 🔐 authorization ⚙️ authentication infrastructure  Identity has therefore become one of the most strategically important layers of enterprise cybersecurity.  ### 🔥 WHY CVSS 10.0 MATTERS  CVSS scores range from:  0.0 → 10.0  A score of:  🚨 **10.0**  represents the maximum technical severity rating.  But severity and real-world risk are not identical.  For this incident, both indicators are strong:  📊 **Severity: Maximum** 🔥 **Threat evidence: Exploitation confirmed**  That combination is much more significant than:  “CVSS 10.0 but nobody has ever exploited it.”  ### 🧠 A CRITICAL DISTINCTION FOR THE HEADLINE  It would be inaccurate to post:  ❌ **“Microsoft Entra ID is currently wide open.”**  or:  ❌ **“All Microsoft accounts can now be hacked.”**  Microsoft explicitly says the vulnerability has already been mitigated.  The accurate story is:  > **Microsoft discovered a maximum-severity Entra ID RCE vulnerability that had been exploited in the wild and says it has now fully mitigated the flaw.**  That is still a major security story.  ### 🕵️ ATTRIBUTION STATUS  Currently:  ❌ No public attacker identified ❌ No public campaign name ❌ No confirmed nation-state attribution ❌ No public exploitation chain ❌ No disclosed victim count ❌ No disclosed scale  Confirmed:  ✅ CVE-2026-69836 ✅ Entra ID affected ✅ unsafe deserialization issue ✅ remote code execution possible ✅ unauthorized network attacker ✅ CVSS 10.0 ✅ exploitation in the wild ✅ Microsoft mitigation deployed ✅ no customer patch required  ### 🧬 CONNECTION TO THE BIGGER MICROSOFT THREAT LANDSCAPE  The disclosure follows another Microsoft security incident earlier in August involving:  **CVE-2026-68820**  a Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock privilege-escalation vulnerability.  THN reports that vulnerability was exploited as a zero-day by the **North Korea-linked Lazarus Group** as part of **Operation Dream Job**.  Important:  ⚠️ **There is currently no evidence in THN's Entra ID report tying Lazarus Group to CVE-2026-69836.**  These are separate security stories.  That's exactly why attribution discipline matters in threat intelligence.  ### 🛡️ WHY THIS MATTERS TO SOC TEAMS  Security teams increasingly have to watch identities the same way they historically watched endpoints.  Traditional SOC model:  💻 endpoint alert ↓ malware identified ↓ machine isolated  Modern identity-centric incident:  👤 account/token anomaly ↓ privileged access ↓ cloud application activity ↓ data access ↓ lateral movement across SaaS/cloud  Useful identity telemetry includes:  🔎 sign-in logs 🔎 conditional-access events 🔎 privileged-role changes 🔎 application consent 🔎 service principals 🔎 token anomalies 🔎 MFA changes 🔎 authentication-method changes 🔎 impossible or unusual travel 🔎 suspicious cloud application access  ### 📌 CURRENT PICTURE  🔴 CVE-2026-69836 🔴 Microsoft Entra ID 🔴 Formerly Azure Active Directory 🔴 CVSS 10.0 🔴 Remote Code Execution 🔴 Unsafe deserialization 🔴 Unauthorized network attacker 🔴 Exploited in the wild 🟢 Microsoft says fully mitigated 🟢 No customer patch required ⚠️ Exploitation details not publicly disclosed ⚠️ Scale currently unknown ⚠️ Threat actor currently unknown  The story is not:  > **“A theoretical Microsoft vulnerability was discovered.”**  It is:  > **Microsoft's cloud identity platform contained a maximum-severity remote-code-execution vulnerability that attackers had already exploited — and Microsoft says it has now neutralized the flaw across the service.**  🔗 **Sources:** The Hacker News • Microsoft Security Response Center  #CyberSecurity #Microsoft #EntraID #AzureAD #CVE202669836 #IdentitySecurity #CloudSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #Vulnerability #CyberAttack #SOC #MicrosoftSecurity #CyberNews

OPSEC failures #2 — 500 days on a server everyone already knew about  On 25 October 2024, Ukraine's CERT named an IP address as APT28 infrastructure — a unit the UK's NCSC assesses is almost certainly GRU 26165.  The operators kept using that server for more than 500 days.  Researchers found an open directory on it in January. Inside: credentials from 244 mailboxes, 2FA seeds lifted from 108 accounts, forwarding rules on 143 mailboxes copying every incoming email to an attacker address, and 11,527 contacts mapped across 2,254 domains. Ukrainian regional prosecutors. The Romanian Air Force. Greece's National Defence General Staff.  The IP never changed. The domain never changed. Of 853 forwarding rules, 826 still pointed at the same burned Proton address.  So why not?  Because they did make changes. They renamed the Sieve rule. They started routing some rules through a typosquatted domain.  The cheap stuff changed. The expensive stuff didn't.  The timing says the same. A file still using the reported filter name is dated seven months after the advisory. The rename appears around a year after. This was never a response to being burned.  Rebuilding infrastructure costs a domain, certificates, hosted payloads, runtime modules, a telemetry sink. Getting named again costs a unit nobody can arrest precisely nothing.  Not a capability ceiling either. Proofpoint tracks a separate GRU-directed operation in the same period rotating infrastructure and running proxy jump boxes. Same sponsor. Different answer.  Then the uncomfortable part.  The Romanian Air Force was the most targeted organisation for persistence. Every attempt failed — their mail server didn't support ManageSieve.  Not advanced detection. Not AI. Not a zero-day.  A missing feature.  They still lost 52 credential sets and the 2FA seeds of 39 accounts. But the persistence, the part that survives a password reset, never landed.  Attackers optimise for what's cheap. Defenders survive on what's already there.  All of this comes from @Huntio  toolkit analysis and @ctrlaltintel  follow-on, which decoded the C2 telemetry. The argument is mine; the findings are theirs.

🚨 Hackers Are Poisoning Hotel Wi-Fi to Steal Microsoft 365 Accounts  ReliaQuest has uncovered a widespread campaign targeting Wi-Fi infrastructure at hotels, conference centers and other shared venues, allowing attackers to redirect travelers to malicious Microsoft 365 infrastructure without compromising their devices or sending phishing emails.  * The campaign has been active since at least June 2026  * Compromised Wi-Fi gateways were identified across multiple U.S. cities as well as India and Saudi Arabia  * Attackers gain administrative control of captive-portal gateways and manipulate DNS responses  * Once a gateway is compromised, users connecting to that Wi-Fi network can be silently redirected to attacker-controlled infrastructure  * ReliaQuest observed Microsoft-themed domains being used to facilitate credential and account compromise  * In some cases, attackers abused Microsoft's device-code authentication flow, potentially obtaining MFA-satisfied Microsoft 365 access through valid OAuth tokens  * WPAD abuse was also attempted in roughly one-third of observed cases, potentially allowing additional application traffic to be routed through attacker-controlled proxies  * Victims connecting to affected gateways came from financial services, legal, healthcare, energy, retail and professional-services organizations  🇷🇺 ReliaQuest says the techniques overlap with tradecraft previously associated with APT28 / Fancy Bear / Forest Blizzard, the Russian military intelligence-linked threat group.  However, researchers are NOT directly attributing this campaign to APT28 because they have not identified direct technical links such as shared infrastructure or code reuse.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: This attack changes the traditional phishing model. The employee doesn't need to click a malicious email or connect to an obviously suspicious website. Compromising infrastructure that users already trust allows attackers to move the interception point from the endpoint to the network itself.  For corporate travelers, ReliaQuest's primary recommendation is straightforward: enforce an always-on, full-tunnel VPN so DNS traffic passes through trusted corporate infrastructure rather than the hotel gateway.  Source: ReliaQuest Threat Research reliaquest.com/blog/threat-s… #DDW #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #APT28 #Microsoft365

Un service étranger n’a pas besoin de connaître les 678 000 dossiers. 👉Il recherche peut-être seulement : 50 militaires ; 30 diplomates ; 100 chercheurs ; 200 ingénieurs ; quelques hauts fonctionnaires ; des spécialistes du nucléaire ; des collaborateurs d’entreprises de défense. 👉La base fiscale lui permet éventuellement de connaître : -adresse personnelle, -situation familiale, -revenu, -patrimoine immobilier, -téléphone, -courriel. 👉Une autre fuite permet d’obtenir : -IBAN, -banque, -date de naissance. Une autre : -enfants, -établissement scolaire. Une autre : -administration d’appartenance. 👉Le service peut alors lancer une attaque extrêmement ciblée. Pas contre 600 000 personnes. Contre une seule. C’est ainsi que des données massives deviennent du renseignement de précision. Encore une fois : 👉il s’agit d’un scénario de risque, pas de la description d’une opération russe démontrée dans l’affaire ZeroBytes. 𝗹𝗮 𝗴𝘂𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 𝘃𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲́𝗲 Il existe enfin un dernier scénario souvent oublié. Une puissance étrangère peut exploiter politiquement un scandale qu’elle n’a pas créé. Supposons que tous les pirates soient français et purement criminels. Les incidents restent réels : -FICOBA compromis. -ANTS compromis. -Tchap compromis. -DGFiP compromise. -Éducation nationale compromise. Un dispositif d’influence étranger peut simplement amplifier ces informations en répétant : « L’État français est incapable de protéger ses citoyens. » Puis : « Ils vous cachent la vérité. » « Toutes vos données ont été volées. » « Votre gouvernement ne contrôle plus rien. » Certaines phrases peuvent partir de faits exacts puis être progressivement exagérées. Le but n’est pas nécessairement de faire croire à une histoire entièrement fausse. 👉Les opérations d’influence les plus efficaces utilisent souvent une vérité réelle comme point de départ, avant d’y ajouter peur, exagération et suspicion. La cyberattaque devient alors seulement la première étape. La véritable cible devient : -la confiance dans les institutions. La diplomatie française considère précisément les cyberopérations russes comme une composante d’un ensemble de menaces hybrides associant cyberactivité, manipulation de l’information et ingérence dans les processus démocratiques. 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟳 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲́𝗷𝗮̀ 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗲̂𝘁𝗲𝘀 La prochaine élection présidentielle française doit se dérouler en 2027. Le communiqué français du 13 juillet 2026 concernant le FSB mentionne explicitement la volonté de la France de contrer les opérations de déstabilisation, y compris à l’approche des élections de 2027. 👉Pourquoi ? Parce qu’une opération moderne peut prendre la forme d’un hack-and-leak. -On pirate. -On récupère des documents. -On attend. Puis on publie au moment politiquement le plus destructeur. Le danger devient encore plus important lorsque des documents authentiques sont mélangés à quelques documents falsifiés. L’existence d’une énorme quantité d’informations vraies rend alors les faux beaucoup plus difficiles à identifier. La France possède déjà l’expérience de 2017 et attribue désormais au GRU l’utilisation d’APT28 dans les tentatives de déstabilisation de ce processus électoral. Voilà pourquoi les immenses bases de données volées ne doivent pas être regardées uniquement à travers le prisme de la fraude bancaire 𝗼𝘂̀ 𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝗻𝗾𝘂𝗲̂𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗱’𝗵𝘂𝗶 ? Pour la DGFiP, une plainte a été déposée et les investigations continuent afin de déterminer précisément l’étendue des extractions. La CNIL a été saisie. Pour l’Éducation nationale, une plainte contre X a été déposée auprès du parquet de Paris ; l’ANSSI et la CNIL ont également été saisies. Le ministère confirmait encore le 18 août 2026 que l’enquête judiciaire se poursuivait et que les expertises concernant les éventuelles données d’élèves n’étaient pas terminées. Pour Tchap, la DINUM poursuit l’analyse des journaux techniques afin de déterminer le périmètre exact des consultations et des données éventuellement exfiltrées. Pour ANTS, l’enquête judiciaire a permis d’identifier au moins un auteur ; le gouvernement évoque le jeune suspect âgé de quinze ans. Les vulnérabilités ont été corrigées ou font l’objet d’un plan de remédiation sous accompagnement de l’ANSSI. Et pour ZeroBytes, l’identité réelle complète des personnes se trouvant derrière le pseudonyme et surtout celle des acheteurs revendiqués restent les grandes inconnues publiques du dossier. 𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗮 𝗰𝗻𝗶𝗹 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲́𝘃𝗲́𝗹𝗲𝗿 La CNIL joue ici un rôle différent de celui de la police. La justice cherche notamment : 👉qui a attaqué ? La CNIL cherche également : les responsables des fichiers avaient-ils mis en place un niveau de sécurité suffisant ? Après une violation, elle peut examiner : -les mesures de protection, -la gestion des habilitations, -la conservation des informations, -la détection de l’incident, -la rapidité de la réaction, et la manière dont les victimes ont été averties. 👉Ce point sera particulièrement important. Car le véritable scandale ne serait pas seulement qu’un pirate ait réussi à entrer. Il faudrait également déterminer si certaines faiblesses étaient connues, prévisibles ou auraient raisonnablement pu être évitées. 𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗶 𝘃𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝘃𝗶𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗻𝗲 La conséquence la plus immédiate de ces fuites n’est probablement pas spectaculaire. 👉Elle est psychologique. Jusqu’à aujourd’hui, lorsqu’un interlocuteur connaissait notre adresse, notre situation fiscale ou une partie de notre dossier administratif, nous pouvions raisonnablement penser : « Il doit réellement travailler pour l’administration. » Ce raisonnement devient dangereux. 👉Le fait qu’une personne connaisse désormais -votre adresse, -votre IBAN, -votre revenu fiscal, -votre enfant, -votre établissement scolaire, ou votre numéro fiscal 👉ne prouve plus qu’elle représente l’organisme dont elle prétend venir. À mesure que les bases se multiplient sur les marchés clandestins, notre ancienne méthode pour distinguer le vrai du faux — « il connaît des informations confidentielles, donc il est légitime » — devient obsolète. 👉C’est peut-être l’un des changements les plus profonds provoqués par cette crise. 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻  𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗔𝗟𝗘 𝗡’𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗣𝗟𝗨𝗦 𝗦𝗘𝗨𝗟𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗤𝗨𝗘 𝗡𝗢𝗦 𝗗𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘́𝗘𝗦 𝗔𝗜𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗘́𝗧𝗘́ 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗘́𝗘𝗦. 𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗖𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗔𝗟𝗘 𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗤𝗨𝗘 𝗡𝗢𝗨𝗦 𝗜𝗚𝗡𝗢𝗥𝗢𝗡𝗦 𝗤𝗨𝗜 𝗙𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗥𝗔 𝗣𝗔𝗥 𝗟𝗘𝗦 𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗦𝗘́𝗗𝗘𝗥. Il faut maintenant regarder l’ensemble. 👉Fin janvier 2026 : FICOBA est consulté frauduleusement après l’usurpation des identifiants d’un fonctionnaire.  👉Environ 1,2 million de comptes bancaires sont concernés. 15 avril 2026 : l’ANTS détecte une intrusion susceptible de concerner 11,7 millions de comptes ; quelques jours plus tard, le ministre de l’Intérieur parle d’environ 11,6 millions de données nominatives exfiltrées. 👉30 avril : le Premier ministre reconnaît environ trois vols de données par jour, une importante dette numérique, des systèmes remontant parfois aux années 1990 et une perméabilité croissante entre acteurs criminels, individus et puissances étrangères. 👉7 juin : un compte Tchap est compromis ; 73 467 agents publics sont potentiellement concernés. 👉25 juillet : nouvelle intrusion à l’Éducation nationale. 👉12 et 13 août : la compromission des systèmes de la DGFiP devient publique ; 678 000 particuliers et professionnels apparaissent dans le premier bilan. 👉La FAQ du fisc révèle ensuite que les informations potentiellement récupérées comprennent bien davantage que le seul revenu fiscal : identifiant fiscal, état civil, téléphone, courriel, situation familiale, personnes à charge, nombre de parts, revenu fiscal de référence, taux de prélèvement à la source et historique des échanges avec l’administration. Et pendant que tout cela se produit, la France accuse officiellement le GRU russe d’avoir utilisé APT28 contre des intérêts français et désigne le 16e Centre du FSB, unité 61240, comme menant des opérations persistantes de cyberespionnage contre notre pays. 👉Voilà pourquoi le dossier est infiniment plus sérieux qu’un simple « piratage du site des impôts ». Il révèle trois crises simultanées. 👉La première est technique : l’État possède encore une dette numérique considérable. 👉La deuxième est criminelle : la donnée personnelle est devenue un marché. 👉Et la troisième est géopolitique : des puissances étrangères cherchent activement à pénétrer les systèmes français et peuvent s’appuyer sur des acteurs non étatiques dans leurs opérations. Il ne faut pas fabriquer un coupable pour rendre l’histoire plus spectaculaire. Nous n’avons aucune preuve que ZeroBytes travaille pour Moscou. C’est précisément parce que le dossier est suffisamment grave sans inventer quoi que ce soit qu’il faut rester rigoureux. Mais nous devons désormais nous poser une question différente. 👉Pas seulement : « Qui a volé ces données ? » Mais : Qui les a copiées ? Qui les conserve ? Qui les revend ? Qui les rachète ? Qui les recoupe avec d’autres bases ? Qui sélectionne certaines personnes ? Qui peut les exploiter dans cinq ans ? Parce qu’une base numérique n’est pas comme un camion rempli de documents. Le camion ne peut être vendu qu’une fois. Une base peut être copiée mille fois. Un pirate peut la vendre aujourd’hui à un fraudeur. Demain à un courtier. Après-demain à un autre criminel. Et rien n’empêche théoriquement qu’une copie finisse un jour entre les mains d’un acteur ayant des motivations entièrement différentes. C’est là que la frontière entre cybercriminalité et sécurité nationale devient dangereusement mince. Nous avons confié à l’État des informations que nous ne confierions probablement jamais toutes ensemble à une entreprise privée : nos revenus, notre domicile, nos comptes, notre patrimoine, notre famille, nos enfants, notre identité. Nous l’avons fait parce que le fonctionnement d’un État moderne l’exige. Mais ce choix repose sur un contrat implicite : l’État collecte parce qu’il protège. Lorsque la protection faiblit, ce contrat de confiance commence à se fissurer. Et il existe une différence fondamentale entre l’argent et l’identité. 👉L’argent volé peut parfois être remboursé. Une carte bancaire peut être remplacée. Un mot de passe peut être changé. Mais personne ne peut changer son passé. Personne ne peut remplacer sa date de naissance. Personne ne peut effacer facilement ses anciennes adresses. Personne ne peut changer le nom de ses enfants. Personne ne peut réinitialiser vingt années d’histoire administrative. C’est pourquoi le véritable héritage de ces attaques peut nous poursuivre beaucoup plus longtemps que leurs auteurs. La grande bataille numérique qui commence ne porte donc pas seulement sur des serveurs. Elle porte sur notre capacité à rester maîtres de notre identité

4/𝗹’𝗲́𝘁𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗮𝗶̂𝘁 𝗮𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶 𝗮𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘂𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗽 𝗺𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶 𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀 Autre chiffre extrêmement révélateur dans le discours du 30 avril. Le Premier ministre estime que de nombreuses entreprises françaises consacrent environ 10 % de leur budget global à leurs infrastructures numériques, alors que l’État serait davantage proche de 1 %. Cette comparaison est approximative et le Premier ministre précise lui-même qu’elle ne doit pas être prise comme une équivalence parfaite. Mais elle sert à illustrer le diagnostic gouvernemental : l’investissement n’a pas suivi la dépendance croissante de l’administration au numérique. 👉Or plus un État numérise : -les impôts, -les identités, -les prestations, -les dossiers scolaires, -les collectivités, -la santé, plus le coût d’une faiblesse augmente. En informatique, la dette technique fonctionne un peu comme une dette financière. Elle peut être ignorée un moment. Mais plus elle s’accumule, plus son remboursement devient coûteux. 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝗲́𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 : 𝟮𝟬𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗱’𝗲𝘂𝗿𝗼𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗲́𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗿𝗲𝘀 Face au constat, le gouvernement annonce un plan d’urgence. 👉Premier élément : 200 millions d’euros supplémentaires doivent financer des investissements dans les applications, les systèmes de détection et notamment la cryptographie post-quantique. Le financement doit notamment provenir de crédits France 2030. La cryptographie post-quantique peut sembler éloignée des attaques par mots de passe qui nous occupent aujourd’hui. Mais elle répond à un autre risque : l’arrivée future d’ordinateurs quantiques suffisamment puissants pourrait fragiliser certains systèmes cryptographiques actuels. Le gouvernement tente donc simultanément de réparer les vulnérabilités présentes et de préparer les défenses de demain. 𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗾 𝗽𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝘂 𝗯𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗲́𝗿𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗱𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲̀𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝗮̀ 𝗹𝗮 𝗰𝘆𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲́𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲́ À partir de 2027, le gouvernement veut imposer que 5 % du budget numérique de chaque ministère soit consacré à la cybersécurité. Il veut également utiliser les amendes prononcées par la CNIL pour créer un fonds de modernisation des infrastructures numériques de l’État. Le Premier ministre évoquait alors environ 500 millions d’euros d’amendes sur l’année précédente, somme qu’il souhaitait recycler dans la sécurisation informatique plutôt que laisser revenir intégralement au budget général. 👉Cette mesure possède une dimension presque ironique : les sanctions infligées pour des défaillances dans la protection des données pourraient désormais contribuer à financer la protection des données publiques. 𝗹’𝗲́𝘁𝗮𝘁 𝘃𝗲𝘂𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲 𝘀𝗲 𝗽𝗶𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝘂𝗶-𝗺𝗲̂𝗺𝗲 Une autre mesure mérite une attention particulière. Le Premier ministre explique avoir donné instruction aux services de sécurité de l’État de mener des « auto-attaques » contre leurs propres systèmes. 👉Le principe est celui du red teaming. Des spécialistes se comportent comme de véritables attaquants. -Ils cherchent : -les portes ouvertes, -les comptes vulnérables, -les erreurs de configuration, -les chemins permettant de passer d’un système à un autre, -les possibilités d’exfiltration. -L’idée est simple : mieux vaut que la France découvre sa propre faille aujourd’hui plutôt qu’un adversaire demain. Le gouvernement veut également utiliser davantage l’intelligence artificielle pour automatiser la recherche de vulnérabilités. 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 : 𝗰𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗶 𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘂𝘃𝗲́ À ce jour : nous ne disposons d’aucune preuve publique permettant de l’affirmer. Mais cela ne signifie absolument pas que la menace russe est imaginaire. 👉Au contraire. Le 29 avril 2025, la France attribue officiellement plusieurs cyberattaques visant ses intérêts au service de renseignement militaire russe, le GRU, utilisant le mode opératoire APT28. Depuis 2021, une dizaine d’entités françaises ont été ciblées ou compromises. Il s’agit notamment : -de services publics, -d’entreprises privées, et d’une organisation sportive liée aux Jeux olympiques et paralympiques de Paris 2024. La France associe également historiquement APT28 au sabotage de TV5Monde en 2015 et à la tentative de déstabilisation du processus électoral français de 2017. APT28 est par ailleurs employé contre l’Ukraine dans le contexte de la guerre menée par la Russie. 👉Cela signifie une chose très simple : la Russie dispose déjà d’une activité cyber offensive documentée contre la France. 𝗹𝗲 𝟭𝟯 𝗷𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲, 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝘀𝗯 Un peu plus d’un mois avant l’explosion publique du scandale DGFiP, la France fait une annonce encore plus importante. Le 13 juillet 2026, elle attribue officiellement des opérations persistantes de cyberespionnage au 16e Centre du FSB, le service fédéral de sécurité russe. 👉Et Paris donne même le numéro de l’unité : 61240. Selon la diplomatie française, cette unité est spécifiquement chargée du ciblage de la France. Le groupe utilise notamment le mode opératoire connu sous le nom de TURLA. Les cibles attribuées à cette structure russe comprennent : -des comptes de messagerie du ministère des Armées depuis 2017 ; -le réseau de l’ambassade de France à Moscou en 2018 ; -un serveur appartenant à une entité du secteur judiciaire en 2019 ; -et, en février 2025, un institut de recherche français spécialisé dans des technologies sensibles et travaillant pour l’industrie de défense. Dans ce dernier cas, la France affirme qu’un volume significatif de données a été exfiltré. Nous ne sommes donc absolument plus dans la spéculation sur l’existence du cyberespionnage russe. 👉Il est officiellement attribué. 𝗹𝗮 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗲́𝗴𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘂𝗻 𝗲́𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲̀𝗺𝗲 𝗱’𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗻 𝗲́𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀 Et voici l’élément qui rend la question ZeroBytes particulièrement intéressante. Dans son communiqué du 13 juillet, la France affirme que la Russie renforce ses capacités cyber offensives tout en s’appuyant sur un écosystème diversifié d’acteurs non étatiques, notamment des groupes se présentant comme « hacktivistes ». Ces acteurs peuvent participer à des opérations de déstabilisation. La France considère ces cyberactivités comme l’une des composantes d’un ensemble plus large de menaces hybrides comprenant également : -la manipulation de l’information, -l’ingérence dans les processus démocratiques, et d’autres opérations de déstabilisation. Le gouvernement prévoit explicitement ce danger dans la perspective des élections françaises de 2027. Mais cela ne prouve toujours pas que ZeroBytes appartient à cet écosystème. 👉La distinction doit rester absolument nette. 𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 𝗹𝘂𝗶-𝗺𝗲̂𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘅𝘆𝘀 Le 30 avril 2026, Sébastien Lecornu développe précisément cette question. 👉Il distingue trois familles : -acteurs étatiques ; organisations criminelles ; individus isolés. Mais il explique que ces catégories étaient autrefois davantage séparées. Aujourd’hui, selon lui, il existe une forte perméabilité entre ces mondes. Après les révélations sur le jeune suspect de l’affaire ANTS, il va encore plus loin. Il explique qu’un individu, une organisation criminelle ou un acteur étatique peuvent éventuellement être instrumentalisés les uns par les autres. Il cite explicitement la Russie et l’Iran comme pays capables de recourir à des proxys afin de compliquer l’attribution des opérations. Cette déclaration ne concerne pas spécifiquement ZeroBytes. 👉Il faut le rappeler. Mais elle démontre que le scénario d’un acteur criminel utilisé directement ou indirectement par un État n’est absolument pas considéré comme fantaisiste par les autorités françaises. 𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗰𝗲́𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗼 𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗹𝘂𝘀 𝗰𝗿𝗲́𝗱𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗻’𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝘂𝘁-𝗲̂𝘁𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀 « 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘂 𝗮 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲́ 𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗶𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 » La question russe est probablement mal formulée lorsqu’on demande simplement : « La Russie a-t-elle piraté la DGFiP ? » 👉Nous n’en avons aucune preuve. Une meilleure question serait : « Une puissance hostile pourrait-elle récupérer ou acheter ensuite des données initialement volées par des criminels indépendants ? » 👉Techniquement, oui. Le marché cyber permet précisément cette séparation des rôles. -Un acteur vole des identifiants. -Un autre les achète. -Un autre pénètre le réseau. -Un autre extrait une base. -Un courtier la revend. -Un acheteur l’exploite. Ces acteurs peuvent ne jamais se rencontrer physiquement. Ils peuvent même se trouver sur plusieurs continents. C’est pourquoi les deux acheteurs revendiqués par ZeroBytes sont potentiellement plus intéressants pour une enquête de renseignement que le discours public des pirates eux-mêmes.

sample_tweets.text: America’s First Chief Ponzi Officer Strikes Again: The New Atkins Rule Deregulates the Most Fraud-Saturated Asset Class in Financial History  The SEC just proposed a sweeping new rule surrendering oversight of crypto. The economic analysis ignores everything that matters: 17 years of failed blockchain deployments, 13 million dead tokens, $17B in crypto crime in 2025 alone, the largest financial theft in history (North Korea, funding its weapons program) and the removal of every crypto guardrail.  The crypto-traceability myth, debunked. The state-regulator backstop, debunked. The financial-inclusion spin, debunked. The self-certification safe harbor, debunked. 글로벌 진출이 핫해진 김에..! 글로벌 진출 팁 간단히  우선 저는 치지직에서 한국어 / 유튜브에서 영어, 일본어, 스페인어 등 / 빌리빌리에서 중국어로 방송하는 놈입니다  1. 외국 팬들을 만들고 싶어요! -> 1순위로 노려야하는건 영어권, 일본입니다 버튜버 팬층이 가장 많고 두터우며 소비력도 있고 한국 문화에도 상대적으로 익숙합니다 한국 오타쿠가 가장 배우기 쉬운 언어들이기도 하구요  2. 그럼 어디서 방송하나요? -> 우선 외국 버튜버들은 주로 유튜브와 트위치에서 방송합니다  하지만 제가 트위치에서 오래 방송해본 결과 한국 시장 철수의 여파로 후원도 받을 수 없고 다시보기도 남지 않고 노래뱅도 한국에서 노출이 안 됩니다 서드파티도 외국인이 쉽게 접근하기 어렵구요  하지만 유튜브는 수익화는 어려워졌다고 하나 한국에서도 잘 서비스 되고 있고 후원을 받기도 쉽습니다 다만 알고리즘 때문에 한국어 영상을 주로 올리고 있다면 따로 채널을 파는걸 추천드립니다 - 저는 노래커버+메인 채널과 각 언어 마다 컨텐츠 영상 올리는 채널이 따로 있습니다 (언어 별로 구글 계정도 다 따로 만드시는게 좋습니다)  3. 영어, 일본어 말고 추천하는 언어가 있나요? -> 중남미의 스페인어 구사자 중에 버튜버 좋아하시는 분들이 많구요, 브라질의 포르투갈어, 인도네시아의 인니어, 태국어도 시청자가 많은 편이라 배워주면 쏠쏠합니다 저는 개인적으로 튀르키예어, 아랍어, 프랑스어, 독일어도 배우고 있습니다 러시아어, 아프리카 쪽 언어도 배워보긴 했는데 러시아가 유튜브 검열이 심해서 소용 없고, 아프리카 쪽은 단 한 명의 시청자도 유입이 없어서 효율이 너무 낮았습니다  4. 중국 본토 진출은 어떤가요? -> 중국 버튜버는 빌리빌리에서 생방송을 진행합니다 하지만 빌리빌리는 외국인의 생방송이 금지되어있습니다 중국 본토의 MCN을 이용해야만 가능합니다 한국 버튜버, 특히 개인세가 중국 MCN에 들어가기란 매우 어렵습니다 일단 한국에 빌리빌리 길드(MCN) 정보가 아예 없습니다.. 저도 중국 활동을 오래 하면서 먼저 MCN에서 제의가 와서 겨우 가능해졌습니다 또한 샤오홍슈도 같이 운영하면 좋습니다 웨이보는 제가 예전에 해킹 당한 뒤로 못 들어가고 있어서 여기 분위기는 모르겠네요..  다만 영상 업로드, 게시글 작성은 가능하니 가볍게 커버 영상 정도 올리는건 괜찮습니다 수익이 없을 뿐이죠..ㅜ 그리고 검열 조심하세요..  마치며 -> 재미있으셨고 도움이 되셨으면 좋겠고 더 궁금한게 있으면 에덴월드를 통해서 멘토링 신청이 가능합니다 감사합니다!

Yes and it's now the dominant attack method.  79% of all cyberattack detections in 2024 involved no malware whatsoever. not 10%. not 30%. 79%.  it's called living off the land. LOLBins. fileless attacks.  here's how it works.  your operating system ships with powerful built-in tools. PowerShell. Windows Management Instrumentation. certutil.exe. mshta.exe. rundll32.exe. legitimate, Microsoft-signed utilities that IT teams use every day.  an attacker gets initial access a phishing email, a stolen credential, a compromised VPN and then never touches a malware file again.  instead they use your own tools against you.  PowerShell downloads and executes code directly in memory. nothing written to disk. certutil.exe a certificate management tool can download files from the internet. WMI can execute commands on remote machines across your entire network.  your antivirus sees PowerShell running. PowerShell runs every day. legitimate. signed by Microsoft. nothing to flag.  the attacker is already inside.  A real world example is Volt Typhoon. A Chinese state-sponsored group. spent years inside US critical infrastructure power grids, water systems, communications networks. CISA confirmed it. No custom malware. They used only tools that shipped with Windows.  Forensics teams found almost nothing to analyze afterward. when memory cleared, the evidence cleared with it.  the defense is behavioral detection. watching not what runs but how and why.  PowerShell running at 3am from a user who never uses it.  certutil downloading a file from an IP in a foreign country.  the tool is legitimate.  the behavior is the attack.

It's always useful to contextualize current events in a framework that is consistent, historically accurate, grounded in material reality, economically literate, morally upright, and philosophically sound.  By design, our society is awash in lies, deceit, half truths, false narratives, and obfuscatory fog. The purpose is to disconnect the masses from reality and allow the ruling class a free hand to pursue their most important interests without any interference from us. Through the proliferation of ignorance and confusion, they become unaccountable shepherds, able to herd their mindless flock into whatever catastrophe they want, without any fear of jeopardizing their status as the ruling class.  Most have no idea what is going on and have become terminally confused with their personal identity inextricably linked to false narratives and ideologies that have nothing at all to do with objective reality. What follows is an effort to bring clarity to current events, a clarity that is nonexistent within the establishment press and is barely found in the alternative media.  First I provide a brief sketch of the four front war for global hegemony that is being waged by the Transnational Western Oligarchy. Then I explain how these events are culminating in one of the most important elections of our time, in one of the most important countries in the world. Then I do my best to explain why this election is a big deal given the context within which it is taking place.  Here's the Cliff's note version for those who want to know what they will be investing their time in:  Shaping the Battlefield: How the U.S. Is Positioning Itself to Contain and Isolate China  I.
